messages:
maddie: Heads up — noticing a subset of edge infer pods still getting traffic after a GPU node drain. API shows endpoints removed but some clients keep resolving old IPs via CoreDNS for ~2-5m. Anyone seen this?

raj: Seen it in us-west-edge during the last autoscale. EndpointSlice looked updated but clients kept the old A records for a bit. Might be CoreDNS caching + kube-proxy/conntrack leftovers.

oliver: Can you paste `kubectl get endpointslices -n infer -o wide` and the CoreDNS logs around the time of scale-down?

maddie: Pasting a snippet (sanitized):
```
NAME                         ENDPOINTS  ADDRESS-TYPE
infer-headless-abcde         3          IPv4
infer-headless-xyz12         1          IPv4
```
CoreDNS tail: `kubernetes:1181: warning: TTL 30 for A record infer-headless.cluster.local -> 10.0.5.12` then later `DELETE endpoint 10.0.5.12` but clients still resolve 10.0.5.12 for ~180s.

anya: Also saw external egress/NAT pain — when clients send to stale IPs, SNAT ket gets held and LB health checks start flapping. We had a couple of 502s.

deploy-bot: [deploy-bot] ScaleDown completed: node gpu-edge-23 removed (2028-11-07T14:21:00Z)

raj: My hunch: kube-proxy didn't garbage-collect the iptables/ipvs rule immediately and conntrack kept NAT mapping. Traffic hits the node IP that no longer has the pod, causing blackhole until conntrack expires (~1-2m). CoreDNS TTL + clients retry make it worse.

oliver: That fits. Which kube-proxy mode are we on for edge clusters? iptables or ipvs? ipvs tends to be quicker to reflect EndpointSlice deletions if the sync loop is tuned.

maddie: iptables on most edge pools. We tried a manual `conntrack -L | grep 10.0.5.12` and found entries. Workaround was `sudo conntrack -D -d 10.0.5.12` on the node and traffic recovered.

ci-bot: [ci-bot] Note: running a quick job to collect conntrack counts from us-west-edge nodes.

anya: Also found CoreDNS cache plugin respecting TTL but some clients (NodeLocal DNS caches + kubelet resolv.conf) keep caches too. Node-local-dns pods had cached A for 60s.

raj: Actionable items I propose: 
- reduce CoreDNS `upstream` cache TTL for headless zones to 5-10s (configmap change)
- enable more aggressive kube-proxy sync (`--conntrack-min`/timeouts) or consider ipvs on edge pools
- add a post-drain hook to run `conntrack -D` for drained pod IPs on the node before removal
- increase EndpointSlice controller QPS/sync if we see controller lag

oliver: +1. Also add Grafana panels: endpoint->pods mismatch, conntrack count over time, node-local-dns cache hit/miss. Could automate `kubectl delete pod -n kube-system node-local-dns-...` as part of scaledown? risky.

maddie: Short term, I patched CoreDNS config for the infer namespace to TTL 8s and added a DaemonSet job that runs `conntrack -D -s <drained-pod-cidr>` after scale events. Testing on a canary pool now.

anya: FYI we also saw LB healthcheck source IPs being SNATed to a stale node due to egress pool assignment; adding a healthcheck retry + fallback to control plane region helped mitigate 502 noise.

raj: Long term: move edge pools to ipvs + enable conntrack maintenance cron on kubelet? And file upstream bug for endpointSlice deletion->notification order if we can reproduce.

maddie: I'll open a short runbook with the mitigation steps + include command snippets:
```
sudo conntrack -D -d 10.0.5.12
kubectl get endpointslices -n infer -o wide
kubectl rollout restart daemonset/kube-proxy -n kube-system  # cautious
```
I'll also add the CoreDNS CM diff to the runbook.

oliver: If canary looks good, roll to other edge pools during low-traffic window.

maddie: Thanks all — tagging @oliver for monitoring dashboards. Will follow up with runbook link in this thread. :thumbsup:
